summary: Creates a central place to record the IPv6 interface identifiers and ranges that other RFCs have reserved or given special meaning, since a node that automatically picks an identifier in one of those ranges could get unexpected results. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some house numbers are saved for special uses. This memo makes one list of those special numbers so nobody grabs one by accident.

questions: which ipv6 interface ids are reserved
what are reserved ipv6 interface identifiers
why can't i use fdff:ffff:ffff:ffff as an interface id
what is the iana registry for reserved iids
subtitle: A registry of IPv6 interface identifiers that automatic address assignment must not hand out.

tldr.problem: Some interface identifiers are reserved by other specifications, for example as anycast addresses, but a node that generates its own identifier could pick one by accident and receive traffic meant for something else.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5453 creates an IANA registry of reserved IPv6 interface identifiers, seeded with the subnet-router anycast identifier and the reserved subnet anycast range, and says these MUST NOT be used for autoconfiguration.
tldr.outcome: Implementers have one place to check. Future assignments from the registry are discouraged and need Standards Action.

today: RFC 5453 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It established the IANA registry of reserved IPv6 interface identifiers.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers in IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
An IPv6 unicast address has two parts: a subnet prefix and an interface identifier (IID) that identifies a unique interface within the subnet prefix. For all unicast addresses except those starting with binary 000, IIDs are required to be 64 bits long and built in Modified EUI-64 format, per RFC 4291.

Some mechanisms generate IIDs without a unique token, including Cryptographically Generated Addresses, privacy addresses and hash-based addresses. Non-unique IIDs can also come from managed assignment such as DHCPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is like a street name plus a house number. The house number part is the interface identifier.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.content: The document applies only to interface identifiers formed in the modified EUI-64 format defined in Appendix A of RFC 4291. Other kinds of identifiers are out of its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is only about house numbers made in one particular way, not every kind.

sections.title: The Problem with Reusing Reserved Identifiers
sections.content:
Suppose a node using temporary addresses comes up with the IID fdff:ffff:ffff:ffff. RFC 2526 reserved that value as the anycast address of a Mobile IPv6 home agent, so the node would receive requests from every node looking for a home agent.

At best that is an annoyance. At worst another node on the link is denied service and may not look for other ways to find a home agent. The RFC therefore states that such reserved IIDs MUST NOT be used for autonomous autoconfiguration or for managed address configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: If you picked the house number the fire department uses, everyone looking for the fire department would knock on your door.

sections.title: Why a Registry
sections.content:
The RFC weighs two ways to stop nodes from using reserved IIDs. One is to add a normative reference to every specification that reserves one. The other is to create an IANA registry.

The reference approach has two disadvantages: it does not scale because the number of specifications to update is large, and the document reserving the IID may be less mature than the one prohibited from using it, causing a downward reference problem. The registry is judged the better solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of telling every rule book about every special number, keep one list that everyone can look at.

sections.title: The Registry and Its Rules
sections.content:
The registry starts with two entries: the all-zero IID 0000:0000:0000:0000 (Subnet-Router Anycast, RFC 4291) and the range FDFF:FFFF:FFFF:FF80 to FDFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF (Reserved Subnet Anycast Addresses, RFC 2526).

Because implementations might predate a new assignment, future assignments are discouraged. Any are made through Standards Action (RFC 5226), and may be a single IID or a range. The RFC also notes that :: as the unspecified address and ::/0 as a default route do not conflict with the registry, since the reserved IIDs exist to avoid conflicts with stateless autoconfiguration over a 64-bit prefix.

An appendix lists RFCs whose implementations should be aware of the reserved ranges when allocating addresses, such as DHCPv6, CGA, stateless autoconfiguration and privacy extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The list starts with two entries and the keepers say they would rather not add more.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: A node that uses one of the reserved IIDs might receive requests it is not authorized to receive. Information that creates or updates an entry in the registry needs to be authenticated and authorized by IANA following the instructions in RFC 5226.
sections.plainLanguage: Using a special number could make you get messages meant for someone else, so only the list keepers may change the list.
